claim: Naturally occurring point mutations in the HBG promoter switch hemoglobin synthesis from defective adult beta-globin to fetal gamma-globin in sickle cell patients with hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH) and ameliorate the clinical severity.
source: Naturally occurring point mutations in the HBG promoter switch hemoglobin synthesis from defective adult beta-globin to fetal gamma-globin in sickle cell patients with hereditary persistence of fetal hemoglobin (HPFH) and ameliorate the clinical severity.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about HPFH and its clinical effects, as well as implicit citation to the broader literature on this topic.

claim: Base editing at –123 and –124 bp of HBG promoter induced fetal hemoglobin (HbF) to a higher level than disruption of well-known BCL11A binding site in erythroblasts derived from human CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC).
source: Base editing at –123 and –124 bp of HBG promoter induced fetal hemoglobin (HbF) to a higher level than disruption of well-known BCL11A binding site in erythroblasts derived from human CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript comparing HbF induction levels between different base editing targets.

claim: The introduction of –123T > C and –124T > C HPFH-like mutations drives gamma-globin expression by creating a de novo binding site for KLF1.
source: We further demonstrated in vitro that the introduction of –123T > C and –124T > C HPFH-like mutations drives gamma-globin expression by creating a de novo binding site for KLF1.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro experimental data including EMSA assays demonstrating KLF1 binding to the mutated sequence.

claim: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is a tetramer consisting of two alpha-globin chains and two gamma-globin chains, which are highly expressed during the fetal stage of human life.
source: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is a tetramer consisting of two alpha-globin chains and two gamma-globin chains, which are highly expressed during the fetal stage of human life.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the structure and expression pattern of fetal hemoglobin, supported by citation (Bauer and Orkin, 2012).

claim: The expression of HbF is silenced progressively after birth until it constitutes only about 1% of total hemoglobin.
source: The expression of HbF is silenced progressively after birth until it constitutes only about 1% of total hemoglobin (Bauer and Orkin, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bauer and Orkin, 2012, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Naturally occurring mutations in the regulatory regions of the gamma-globin (HBG) genes have been shown to reactivate expression and increase HbF levels during adult life.
source: Naturally occurring mutations in the regulatory regions of the gamma-globin (HBG) genes have been shown to reactivate expression and increase HbF levels during adult life (Jacob and Raper, 1958).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jacob and Raper, 1958, representing historical scientific findings.

claim: Individuals who inherit HPFH alongside other genetic disorders affecting the adult beta-globin gene, such as sickle cell disease or beta-thalassemia, were shown to have fewer, if any, symptoms.
source: Individuals, who inherit HPFH alongside other genetic disorders affecting the adult beta-globin gene, such as sickle cell disease or beta-thalassemia, were shown to have fewer, if any, symptoms (Jacob and Raper, 1958; Thein, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jacob and Raper, 1958 and Thein, 2018, representing established clinical observations.

claim: High levels of HbF expression have been shown to be beneficial for improving the clinical outcomes of patients with sickle cell anemia and beta-thalassemia.
source: Hence, high levels of HbF expression have been shown to be beneficial for improving the clinical outcomes of patients with sickle cell anemia and beta-thalassemia.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the previous statements and established clinical knowledge about the therapeutic benefit of HbF.

claim: The –175T > C, –198T > C and –113A > G HPFH point mutations create de novo binding sites for the erythroid master regulators TAL1, KLF1, and GATA1, respectively.
source: For example, the –175T > C, –198T > C and –113A > G HPFH point mutations create de novo binding sites for the erythroid master regulators TAL1, KLF1, and GATA1, respectively (Fischer and Nowock, 1990; Martyn et al., 2019; Stoming et al., 1989; Wienert et al., 2017; Wienert et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Fischer and Nowock, 1990; Martyn et al., 2019; Stoming et al., 1989; Wienert et al., 2017; Wienert et al., 2015) documenting these specific mutations and their effects.

claim: The introduction of HPFH-associated mutations around –115 bp from the transcription start site (TSS) of HBG (–114C > A, –117G > A, and a 13 bp deletion [∆13 bp]), and around –200 bp from the TSS (–195C > G, –196C > T, –197C > T, –201C > T and –202C > T/G), were shown to disrupt the binding sites of the two major fetal globin repressors, BCL11A and ZBTB7A/LRF, respectively.
source: Similarly, the introduction of HPFH-associated mutations around –115 bp from the transcription start site (TSS) of HBG (–114C > A, –117G > A, and a 13 bp deletion [∆13 bp]), and around –200 bp from the TSS (–195C > G, –196C > T, –197C > T, –201C > T and –202C > T/G), were shown to disrupt the binding sites of the two major fetal globin repressors, BCL11A and ZBTB7A/LRF, respectively (Martyn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martyn et al., 2018, documenting the effects of these mutations on repressor binding.

claim: Targeted introduction of HPFH mutations into the HBG promoter by nuclease-mediated homology-directed repair is relatively inefficient and can result in high rates of random insertions and deletions (indels) through non-homologous end-joining DNA repair pathways.
source: Targeted introduction of HPFH mutations into the HBG promoter by nuclease-mediated homology-directed repair is relatively inefficient and can result in high rates of random insertions and deletions (indels) through non-homologous end-joining DNA repair pathways (Cavazzana et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cavazzana et al., 2017, documenting the limitations of nuclease-mediated approaches.

claim: Due to the high homology between the duplicated HBG1 and HBG2 genes, simultaneous editing of both HBG promoters by programmable nucleases that cause double-stranded breaks (DSBs) sometimes results in ~4.9 kb deletion comprising the HBG intergenic region with uncertain consequences.
source: In addition, due to the high homology between the duplicated HBG1 and HBG2 genes, simultaneous editing of both HBG promoters by programmable nucleases that cause double-stranded breaks (DSBs) sometimes results in ~4.9 kb deletion comprising the HBG intergenic region with uncertain consequences (Li et al., 2018; Métais et al., 2019; Wienert et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2018; Métais et al., 2019; Wienert et al., 2017, documenting this deletion phenomenon.

claim: Base editing using adenine and cytosine base editors (ABEs and CBEs, respectively) is highly efficient in creating point mutations without inducing high levels of indels.
source: Similar to previous findings, we observed that base editing using adenine and cytosine base editors (ABEs and CBEs, respectively) is highly efficient in creating point mutations without inducing high levels of indels (Gaudelli et al., 2017; Komor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gaudelli et al., 2017 and Komor et al., 2016, as well as data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The vector copy number (VCN) of HUDEP-2 cells transduced with ABE, CBE, or Cas9 lentiviral constructs ranged from 0.25 to 0.85 by real-time PCR.
source: The vector copy number (VCN) of HUDEP-2 cells transduced with ABE, CBE, or Cas9 lentiviral constructs ranged from 0.25 to 0.85 by real-time PCR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The editing efficiency was 88% for Cas9, 10–51% for ABE, and 59–73% for CBE, with the transduction efficiency (as measured by GFP expression) greater than 98%.
source: The editing efficiency was 88% for Cas9, 10–51% for ABE, and 59–73% for CBE, with the transduction efficiency (as measured by GFP expression) greater than 98% (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: After differentiating the cells into erythroid progenitors, the percentage of HbF positive cells was higher in case of ABE and CBE than Cas9.
source: After differentiating the cells into erythroid progenitors, the percentage of HbF positive cells was higher in case of ABE and CBE than Cas9 (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The 4.9 kb deletion was observed at a high frequency (76%) in Cas9 edited cells.
source: As expected, the 4.9 kb deletion was observed at a high frequency (76%) in Cas9 edited cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Some deletions were noted in base edited samples but significantly fewer than with Cas9.
source: We also noted some deletions in base edited samples but significantly fewer than with Cas9 (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The globin chain analysis by RP-HPLC showed lower levels of G gamma but not A gamma chain only in Cas9 edited cells in comparison to ABE and CBE edited cells after normalizing to the control.
source: Consistent with the frequency of the 4.9 kb deletion, the globin chain analysis by RP-HPLC showed lower levels of G gamma but not A gamma chain only in Cas9 edited cells in comparison to ABE and CBE edited cells after normalizing to the control (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: ABE and CBE are highly efficient in editing the highly homologous regions like gamma-globin promoter without causing a large deletion between the two HBG genes.
source: These results suggest that ABE and CBE are highly efficient in editing the highly homologous regions like gamma-globin promoter without causing a large deletion between the two HBG genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data showing lower deletion frequencies with base editors compared to Cas9.

claim: Transcriptomic analysis of the stable cell lines expressing ABE and CBE showed a significant correlation with the wild type HUDEP-2 cells, confirming that the gene expression profiles are not altered.
source: Transcriptomic analysis of the stable cell lines expressing ABE and CBE showed a significant correlation with the wild type HUDEP-2 cells, confirming that the gene expression profiles are not altered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The editing efficiency and HbF levels in both ABE and CBE increases over time with no discernable effect on erythroid differentiation.
source: The editing efficiency and HbF levels in both ABE and CBE increases over time with no discernable effect on erythroid differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c-h).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c-h.

claim: Among the 41 gRNAs designed, 36 gRNAs had a base editing window for ABE, and 32 gRNAs had a base editing window for CBE.
source: Among the 41 gRNAs designed, 36 gRNAs had a base editing window for ABE, and 32 gRNAs had a base editing window for CBE (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the gRNA design data presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The mean transduction efficiency for all these gRNAs in both ABE and CBE samples were around 97%.
source: The mean transduction efficiency for all these gRNAs in both ABE and CBE samples were around 97%.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data measuring GFP expression as a marker of transduction.

claim: The total base editing efficiency (overall conversion achieved by a gRNA) varied from 12% to 81% and 13% to 80% for ABE (n = 30) and CBE (n = 25) respectively as determined by CRISPResso-2 analysis.
source: After excluding the low editing gRNAs, the total base editing efficiency (overall conversion achieved by a gRNA) varied from 12% to 81% and 13% to 80% for ABE (n = 30) and CBE (n = 25) respectively (Figure 2c and d) as determined by CRISPResso-2 analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by NGS data analyzed with CRISPResso-2 and shown in Figure 2c and d.

claim: The individual base conversion frequency (base conversion at single base pair resolution) of ABE (A:T to G:C) and CBE (C:G to T:A) ranged from 0% to 74% and 0% to 61%, respectively.
source: The individual base conversion frequency (base conversion at single base pair resolution) of ABE (A:T to G:C) and CBE (C:G to T:A) ranged from 0% to 74% and 0% to 61%, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and c).
evidence: This claim is supported by NGS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and c.

claim: The average editing efficiency observed was high (>30%) in the canonical positions for ABE (A5-A7) and CBE (C5-C7), while it varied between 1% to 27% in the non-canonical positions for ABE (A1-A4, A8-A12) and CBE (C1-C4, C8-C16) for the different gRNAs used in this study.
source: The average editing efficiency observed was high (>30%) in the canonical positions for ABE (A5-A7) and CBE (C5-C7), while it varied between 1% to 27% in the non-canonical positions for ABE (A1-A4, A8-A12) and CBE (C1-C4, C8-C16) for the different gRNAs used in this study (Figure 2—figure supplement 2e-f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2e-f analyzing positional effects on editing efficiency.

claim: Most of the gRNAs in CBE transduced cells showed unanticipated C- to non-T edits (C-R/G-Y), among which C-to-G conversion was predominant.
source: Most of the gRNAs in CBE transduced cells showed unanticipated C- to non-T edits (C-R/G-Y), among which C-to-G conversion was predominant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data analyzing product purity of CBE editing.

claim: In the case of ABE, we observed a minimal level of unexpected base conversions (A-Y/T-R) at a few on-target sites, consistent with previous studies.
source: In the case of ABE, we observed a minimal level of unexpected base conversions (A-Y/T-R) at a few on-target sites, consistent with previous studies (Gaudelli et al., 2017; Komor et al., 2016, Figure 2—figure supplement 2a-b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a-b and citations to Gaudelli et al., 2017 and Komor et al., 2016.

claim: The indel frequency obtained from deep sequencing data was less than 2% in both ABE and CBE.
source: The indel frequency obtained from deep sequencing data was less than 2% in both ABE and CBE (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c-d).
evidence: This claim is supported by NGS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c-d.

claim: ABE exhibits higher product purity and lower indel frequency than CBE in all cases.
source: Our results suggest that ABE exhibits higher product purity and lower indel frequency than CBE in all cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data comparing ABE and CBE editing outcomes.

claim: The percentage of HbF positive cells ranged from 2% to 44% in ABE and 1% to 35% in CBE.
source: The percentage of HbF positive cells ranged from 2% to 44% in ABE and 1% to 35% in CBE (Figure 2c–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2c–d.

claim: Among the 30 gRNAs in ABE and 25 gRNAs in CBE that we have screened for editing the HBG promoter region, five gRNAs in ABE and one gRNA in CBE showed a greater increase in the number of HbF positive cells (in a range of 40–50%).
source: In our preliminary analysis, among the 30 gRNAs in ABE and 25 gRNAs in CBE that we have screened for editing the HBG promoter region, five gRNAs in ABE and one gRNA in CBE showed a greater increase in the number of HbF positive cells (in a range of 40–50%).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data from the screening experiment.

claim: The transduced gRNAs in K562 cell lines did not result in any decrease in the number of HbF positive cells (98% of cells were HbF positive) suggesting that the targeted regions did not have binding sites for essential transcriptional activators.
source: However, we did not observe any decrease in the number of HbF positive cells (98% of cells were HbF positive) in any of the samples suggesting that the targeted regions did not have binding sites for essential transcriptional activators (Figure 2—figure supplement 3c-d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from K562 cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3c-d and inference about the absence of activator binding sites.

claim: The gRNAs-2, -3, and -4 recreates the well-known naturally occurring HPFH mutations –114C > T, –117G > A, −175T > C and –198T > C.
source: The gRNAs-2, -3, and -4 recreates the well-known naturally occurring HPFH mutations –114C > T, –117G > A, −175T > C and –198T > C (Liu et al., 2018; Martyn et al., 2018; Stoming et al., 1989; Wienert et al., 2018; Wienert et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2018; Martyn et al., 2018; Stoming et al., 1989; Wienert et al., 2018; Wienert et al., 2017 documenting these known HPFH mutations.

claim: Out of the top eight gRNAs identified from the base editor screen, five gRNAs (gRNA-2, gRNA-10, gRNA-11, gRNA-32, and gRNA-34) were common in both ABE and CBE, indicating that these target regions might play an important role in HBG silencing.
source: Out of the top eight gRNAs identified from the base editor screen, five gRNAs (gRNA-2, gRNA-10, gRNA-11, gRNA-32, and gRNA-34) were common in both ABE and CBE, indicating that these target regions might play an important role in HBG silencing.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the screening data showing these gRNAs were effective with both base editors.

claim: The total editing efficiency ranged from 24% to 78% and 36% to 85% with mean transduction efficiencies of 96% and 90% for ABE and CBE, respectively.
source: Corresponding to the screening results, the total editing efficiency ranged from 24% to 78% and 36% to 85% with mean transduction efficiencies of 96% and 90% for ABE and CBE, respectively (Figure 3a–b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a–b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Individual base conversion of A- to-G (ranging from 0% to 65%) or C- to -T (ranging from 1% to 57%) was observed at the respective target regions with less than 2% indel frequency.
source: We observed individual base conversion of A- to-G (ranging from 0% to 65%) or C- to -T (ranging from 1% to 57%) at the respective target regions with less than 2% indel frequency (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b and e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b and e.

claim: Undesired non-C-to-T conversions (i.e., C- to-A or C-to-G) were observed at the on-target site by CBE but not with ABE.
source: Further, we also observed the undesired non-C-to-T conversions (i.e., C- to-A or C-to-G) at the on-target site by CBE but not with ABE (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a-b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a-b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2a-b.

claim: ABE showed higher base editing efficiencies of the cognate A and Ts than the bystander A and Ts for the creation of HPFH mutations.
source: ABE showed higher base editing efficiencies of the cognate A and Ts (A113 and A116 for gRNA-02, T175 for gRNA-03, T198 for gRNA-04) than the bystander A and Ts (A110 and A112 for gRNA-02, T181 for gRNA-03, T199 for gRNA-04) for the creation of HPFH mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing editing efficiency at different positions.

claim: CBE showed C-to-T base conversion at the nucleotides adjacent to the protospacer sequence as previously observed.
source: In the case of CBE, we also observed the C-to-T base conversion at the nucleotides adjacent to the protospacer sequence as previously observed (Arbab et al., 2020; Webber et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Arbab et al., 2020 and Webber et al., 2019 documenting this phenomenon.

claim: Base editing rates were highly similar and there is no variation in base substitution efficiency between the highly homologous HBG1 and HBG2 promoters.
source: Our analysis showed that base editing rates were highly similar and there is no variation in base substitution efficiency between the highly homologous HBG1 and HBG2 promoters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c-d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c-d analyzing editing in HBG1 vs HBG2.

claim: A significant increase in the HBG mRNA expression was observed for all the top eight gRNAs in ABE edited cells (p < 0.01 - p < 0.0001).
source: We observed a significant increase in the HBG mRNA expression for all the top eight gRNAs in ABE edited cells (p < 0.01 - p < 0.0001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a.

claim: In the case of CBE, gRNAs -2, -10, -11, and-42 showed a substantial increase in HBG mRNA expression (p < 0.05 - p < 0.0001), while gRNAs -16, -21, -32, and -34 showed a modest level of expression as compared with the control.
source: In the case of CBE, gRNAs -2, -10, -11, and-42 showed a substantial increase in HBG mRNA expression (p < 0.05 - p < 0.0001), while gRNAs -16, -21, -32, and -34 showed a modest level of expression as compared with the control (Figure 3—figure supplement 3g) before differentiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3g.

claim: The percentage of double positive cells was 83–90% for CBE and above 95% for ABE edited cells compared to the control, which was 77% and 97%, respectively, suggesting that the differentiation ability of the edited cells was not affected.
source: The percentage of double positive cells was 83–90% for CBE and above 95% for ABE edited cells compared to the control, which was 77% and 97%, respectively, suggesting that the differentiation ability of the edited cells was not affected (Figure 3—figure supplement 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 3j).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 3j and inference about differentiation capacity.

claim: A significant induction of gamma-globin chain expression was observed, which represented 10% to30% of total beta-like globin content in all the ABE edited samples (gRNAs -2, -3, -4, -10, -11, -15, -32, and -34).
source: We observed a significant induction of gamma-globin chain expression, which represented 10% to30% of total beta-like globin content in all the ABE edited samples (gRNAs -2, -3, -4, -10, -11, -15, -32, and -34) (Figure 3g).
evidence: This claim is supported by RP-HPLC data shown in Figure 3g.

claim: In the case of CBE, the gamma-globin chain levels were around 6% to45% of total beta-like globin content, among which gRNAs -2, -42, -10, and -11 showed significant elevation when compared to the control.
source: In the case of CBE, the gamma-globin chain levels were around 6% to45% of total beta-like globin content, among which gRNAs -2, -42, -10, and -11 showed significant elevation when compared to the control (Figure 3h).
evidence: This claim is supported by RP-HPLC data shown in Figure 3h.

claim: In both ABE and CBE edited cells, the increase in gamma-globin chains was consistently associated with a reciprocal reduction in beta-globin chains thereby maintaining the alpha to beta-like globin chain ratio.
source: In both ABE and CBE edited cells, the increase in gamma-globin chains was consistently associated with a reciprocal reduction in beta-globin chains thereby maintaining the alpha to beta-like globin chain ratio (Figure 3—figure supplement 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 3i).
evidence: This claim is supported by RP-HPLC data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 3i.

claim: The frequency of 4.9 kb deletion in ABE ranged from 2% to 32% while in CBE it ranged from 0% to 12%.
source: Interestingly, the frequency of 4.9 kb deletion in ABE ranged from 2% to 32% while in CBE it ranged from 0% to 12% (Figure 3—figure supplement 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 3k).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3e and Figure 3—figure supplement 3k.

claim: A high correlation (r = 0.71) was observed between the reduction in HBG2 chain expression and the frequency of large deletion in the case of ABE, whereas much lower correlation was observed with CBE (r = 0.26).
source: We observed a high correlation (r = 0.71) in the case of ABE, whereas much lower correlation was observed with CBE (r = 0.26) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 3i).
evidence: This claim is supported by Pearson correlation analysis of data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 3i.

claim: The reduction in G gamma chain expression is due to higher frequency of deletions in the ABE edited samples, while in the case of CBE, the decrease in the G gamma chain expression is independent of larger deletions and might be due to the biased expression of gamma-globin.
source: These data suggest that the reduction in G gamma chain expression is due to higher frequency of deletions in the ABE edited samples, while in the case of CBE, the decrease in the G gamma chain expression is independent of larger deletions and might be due to the biased expression of gamma-globin.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the correlation analysis and experimental data.

claim: A significant induction of HbF was observed in all the top eight target gRNA transduced cells in ABE (gRNAs- 2, -3, -4, -10, -11, -15, -32, and -34), whereas only gRNA-2, -10, -11, and -42 expressed higher levels of HbF in CBE edited cells.
source: We observed a significant induction of HbF in all the top eight target gRNA transduced cells in ABE (gRNAs- 2, -3, -4, -10, -11, -15, -32, and -34), whereas only gRNA-2, -10, -11, and -42 expressed higher levels of HbF in CBE edited cells (Figure 3e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 3e–f.

claim: The increase in HbF variant is associated with compensatory downregulation of adult hemoglobin levels in the edited cells.
source: Consistent with globin chain analysis, we observed that the increase in HbF variant is associated with compensatory downregulation of adult hemoglobin levels in the edited cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC data showing reciprocal changes in HbF and adult hemoglobin.

claim: Among the validated top eight gRNAs in ABE and CBE, gRNA-2, -10, -11 with ABE and gRNA-2 with CBE resulted in a high target editing efficiency with a corresponding increase in HbF expression.
source: Among the validated top eight gRNAs in ABE and CBE, gRNA-2, -10, -11 with ABE and gRNA-2 with CBE resulted in a high target editing efficiency with a corresponding increase in HbF expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the relationship between editing efficiency and HbF expression across different gRNAs.

claim: A high percentage of base substitution at the target site (more than 95%) was observed with ABE8e with the corresponding increase in the HbF positive cells and gamma-globin chains in both gRNA-03 and -11.
source: We observed a high percentage of base substitution at the target site (more than 95%) with the corresponding increase in the HbF positive cells and gamma-globin chains in both the gRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 4a-c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4a-c using ABE8e.

claim: The frequency of larger deletions was significantly reduced with ABE8e perhaps because of the higher processive rate of ABE8e.
source: The frequency of larger deletions was also significantly reduced perhaps because of the higher processive rate of ABE8e (Figure 3—figure supplement 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4d and inference about the mechanism.

claim: Base editing at –114C > T, –115C > T and –116A > G mutations disrupts the binding of BCL11A and the base conversion at –198T > C and –199T > C affect the binding of LRF/ZBTB7A to the HBG promoter.
source: Base editing of –114C > T, –115C > T and –116A > G mutations disrupts the binding of BCL11A and the base conversion at –198T > C and –199T > C affect the binding of LRF/ZBTB7A to the HBG promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about these mutations and their effects on transcription factor binding.

claim: The installation of –113A > G and –198T > C mutations by gRNA-2 and gRNA-4, generate a binding site for GATA1 and KLF-1, respectively.
source: Further, the installation of –113A > G and –198T > C mutations by gRNA-2 and gRNA-4, generate a binding site for GATA1 and KLF-1, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about these mutations creating transcription factor binding sites.

claim: The base conversion at −175T > C by gRNA-3 (with ABE) creates a TAL1 binding site.
source: Moreover, the base conversion at −175T > C by gRNA-3 (with ABE) creates a TAL1 binding site.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about this mutation creating a TAL1 binding site.

claim: The novel gamma-globin regulatory region identified includes the target base substitution mediated by gRNA-10, -11, -15, -21, -32, and -34 with ABE or CBE.
source: The novel gamma-globin regulatory region identified includes the target base substitution mediated by gRNA-10, -11, -15, -21, -32, and -34 with ABE or CBE.
evidence: This claim is supported by the screening data identifying these novel regulatory regions.

claim: With gRNAs -10 and -11, ABE converts nucleotide at –123T > C and –124T > C position, whereas CBE converts nucleotide at –122G > A (on-target editing site) and –117G > A (outside the editing window) positions.
source: With gRNAs -10 and -11, ABE converts nucleotide at –123T > C and –124T > C position, whereas CBE converts nucleotide at –122G > A (on-target editing site) and –117G > A (outside the editing window) positions.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data showing the specific base conversions achieved by these gRNAs.

claim: Target base substitutions at –123T > C and –124T > C positions result in greater induction of HBG expression, equivalent to that of the known HPFH mutations that disrupt the binding of BCL11A.
source: Target base substitutions at –123T > C and –124T > C positions result in greater induction of HBG expression, equivalent to that of the known HPFH mutations that disrupt the binding of BCL11A.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing HbF induction levels between the novel mutations and known BCL11A-disrupting mutations.

claim: Electroporation of the ABE8e mRNA with gRNA targeting the BCL11A binding site (gRNA-2) and –123 novel cluster (gRNA-11) effectively generated highly efficient base editing at the target site in CD34+ HSPCs from healthy donor.
source: Electroporation of the ABE8e mRNA with gRNA targeting the BCL11A binding site (gRNA-2) and –123 novel cluster (gRNA-11) effectively generated highly efficient base editing at the target site.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CD34+ HSPC editing experiments.

claim: The editing efficiency observed at individual base positions were –110 (31%), –112 (37%), –113 (80%), and –116 (66%) with gRNA-2 and –123 (89%), –124 (91%) with gRNA-11 in CD34+ HSPCs.
source: The editing efficiency observed at individual base positions were –110 (31%), –112 (37%), –113 (80%), and –116 (66%) with gRNA-2 and –123 (89%), –124 (91%) with gRNA-11 (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 4b from CD34+ HSPC experiments.

claim: The relative levels of HBG expression were significantly higher in gRNA-11 (>6-fold) and gRNA-2 (>5-fold) edited samples when compared to control (AAVS1 edited sample) by qRT-PCR in erythroblasts derived from CD34+ HSPCs.
source: The relative levels of HBG expression were significantly higher in gRNA-11 (>6-fold) and gRNA-2 (>5-fold) edited samples when compared to control (AAVS1 edited sample) by qRT-PCR (Figure 4d).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4d from CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroblasts.

claim: A significant downregulation of HBB and unchanged levels of HBA expression were observed in both the tested targets in erythroblasts derived from CD34+ HSPCs.
source: In contrast, a significant downregulation of HBB and unchanged levels of HBA expression were observed in both the tested targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroblasts.

claim: Flow cytometry and HPLC variant analysis confirmed the robust increase in the proportion of HbF positive cells and their HbF content compared with control samples for all the tested targets, with the higher effect in gRNA-11 in erythroblasts derived from CD34+ HSPCs.
source: Flow cytometry and HPLC variant analysis confirmed the robust increase in the proportion of HbF positive cells and their HbF content compared with control samples for all the tested targets, with the higher effect in gRNA-11 (Figure 4e and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and HPLC data shown in Figure 4e and g from CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroblasts.

claim: The globin chain analysis showed an increase in expression of HBG1 and HBG2 globin chain levels and a reduction of HBB globin chain level in erythroblasts derived from base edited CD34+ HSPCs.
source: The globin chain analysis showed an increase in expression of HBG1 and HBG2 globin chain levels and a reduction of HBB globin chain level (Figure 4f).
evidence: This claim is supported by RP-HPLC data shown in Figure 4f from CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroblasts.

claim: Base editing of the HBG proximal promoter with gRNA-2 or -11 did not alter enucleation potential or the expression of erythroid maturation markers CD235a or CD71 in erythroblasts derived from CD34+ HSPCs.
source: Importantly, base editing of the HBG proximal promoter with gRNA-2 or -11 did not alter enucleation potential or the expression of erythroid maturation markers CD235a or CD71 (Figure 4h–i).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4h–i from CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroblasts.

claim: A very minimal frequency of the 4.9 kb deletion was observed in CD34+ HSPCs electroporated with ABE8e and gRNA-2 or -11, which might be due to higher processivity and transient expression of the base editor mRNA.
source: Finally, we determined the frequency of the 4.9 kb deletion in CD34+ HSPCs electroporated with ABE8e and gRNA-2 or -11. We observed a very minimal frequency of the 4.9 kb deletion which might be due to higher processivity and transient expression of the base editor mRNA (Figure 4c).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4c and inference about the mechanism.

claim: The level of HbF induction mediated by the installation of novel –123 cluster HPFH-like mutations (through gRNA-11) is comparable to the naturally occurring –115 cluster HPFH mutations (through gRNA-2) that disrupt the binding site of BCL11A.
source: The present results suggest that the level of HbF induction mediated by the installation of novel –123 cluster HPFH-like mutations (through gRNA-11) is comparable to the naturally occurring –115 cluster HPFH mutations (through gRNA-2) that disrupt the binding site of BCL11A.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data comparing HbF induction levels in CD34+ HSPCs.

claim: Adenine base editing of the HBG1 and HBG2 promoters to recreate the novel –123 cluster HPFH-like mutations is a potential approach for the therapeutic induction of fetal globin level and treatment for beta-hemoglobinopathies.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that adenine base editing of the HBG1 and HBG2 promoters to recreate the novel –123 cluster HPFH-like mutations is a potential approach for the therapeutic induction of fetal globin level and treatment for beta-hemoglobinopathies.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from all the experimental data demonstrating therapeutic-level HbF induction.

claim: The base editing at –123T > C and –124T > C sites by ABE creates the consensus binding site for the master erythroid transcription factor KLF1.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the base editing at –123T > C and –124T > C sites by ABE with a single gRNA creates the consensus binding site for the master erythroid transcription factor KLF1 (Figure 5a and b; Tallack et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and citation to Tallack et al., 2010 defining the KLF1 consensus binding site.

claim: Modest but clear binding of KLF1 to the –123T > C and –124T > C mutated probe was observed in EMSA but not with the wild type probe.
source: We observed modest but clear binding of KLF1 to the –123T > C and –124T > C mutated probe in EMSA but not with the wild type probe (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-b) or probes containing either –123T > C or –124T > C mutations alone (Figure 5c–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5c–d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-b.

claim: The combination of –123T > C and –124T > C mutation is important for the KLF1 binding to the HBG promoter.
source: This confirms that the combination of –123T > C and –124T > C mutation is important for the KLF1 binding to the HBG promoter.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the EMSA data showing binding only with the double mutant.

claim: A weak increase in the signal of KLF1 binding to the HBG promoters was observed in the cells edited to contain the –123 and –124 mutations by ChIP, but the effect was modest.
source: We observed a weak increase in the signal of KLF1 binding to the HBG promoters in the cells edited to contain the –123 and –124 mutations, but the effect was modest, and a similarly weak enhancement was also observed at an arbitrary negative control locus, VEGF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The KLF1 binding is at best weak and may be below the level of detection by ChIP.
source: Thus, as seen in the EMSA, the KLF1 binding is at best weak and may be below the level of detection by ChIP.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the weak ChIP signal.

claim: Despite the higher on-target efficiency, off-target editing was not observed at the top target sites for gRNA-11 with ABE.
source: Despite the higher on-target efficiency, off-target editing was not observed at the top target sites (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is supported by NGS data of predicted off-target sites shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The distribution frequency of A-to- I (in ABE) or C-to-U (in CBE) conversion across the base edited samples was very similar to that of the parental stable cell line.
source: The distribution frequency of A-to- I (in ABE) or C-to-U (in CBE) conversion across the base edited samples was very similar to that of the parental stable cell line (Figure 6b–e).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6b–e.

claim: There is no significant difference between the edited and control cells except for both gamma- and delta-globin genes in differential gene expression analysis.
source: We observed that there is no significant difference between the edited and control cells except for both gamma- and delta-globin genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: ABE and CBE are useful in creating specific point mutations in the homologous HBG1 and HBG2 promoters, leading to a potential increase in the number of HbF positive cells and overall HbF production with a significant reduction in the larger deletion frequency.
source: Overall, these results support that the ABE and CBE are useful in creating specific point mutations in the homologous HBG1 and HBG2 promoters, leading to a potential increase in the number of HbF positive cells and overall HbF production with a significant reduction in the larger deletion frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Current approaches to studying fetal globin regulation by programmable nucleases often result in the deletion of the HBG2 gene due to the introduction of DSBs in both HBG promoters.
source: Current approaches to studying fetal globin regulation by programmable nucleases often result in the deletion of the HBG2 gene due to the introduction of DSBs in both HBG promoters (Traxler et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Traxler et al., 2016 documenting this limitation.

claim: The elimination of the 4.9 kb intergenic region (including the HBG2 gene) appears to allow the locus control region (LCR) to directly interact with the HBG1 promoter and drive its expression.
source: The elimination of the 4.9 kb intergenic region (including the HBG2 gene) appears to allow the locus control region (LCR) to directly interact with the HBG1 promoter and drive its expression (Métais et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Métais et al., 2019 describing this mechanism.

claim: A base editing strategy converts target bases in the editing window without the generation of DSBs and hence largely avoids splicing of the HBG locus.
source: A base editing strategy converts target bases in the editing window without the generation of DSBs and hence largely avoids splicing of the HBG locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about base editing mechanisms and data from the manuscript.

claim: The larger deletions may be mainly a result of simultaneous CRISPR-Cas9-induced DSBs or by paired nickase-mediated two single-strand breaks (SSBs) on opposite DNA strands of the HBG1 and HBG2 gene.
source: The larger deletions may be mainly a result of simultaneous CRISPR-Cas9-induced DSBs or by paired nickase-mediated two single-strand breaks (SSBs) on opposite DNA strands of the HBG1 and HBG2 gene (Ran et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ran et al., 2013a and speculation about the mechanism of deletion formation.

claim: Recent studies have shown the possibility of adjacent SSB on the same DNA strand leading to the formation of genomic deletions in plants.
source: Interestingly, recent studies have shown the possibility of adjacent SSB on the same DNA strand leading to the formation of genomic deletions in plants. The deletion frequency depends upon the initial release of the single-stranded fragment between the two SSBs (Schiml et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schiml et al., 2016 documenting this phenomenon in plants.

claim: The conversion of the persistent nick into DSBs by the replication fork has been reported, where the R-loop primed replication fork encounters the single-strand nick site in DNA template and collapses to produce a DSB.
source: Further reports suggest the conversion of the persistent nick into DSBs by the replication fork. The R-loop primed replication fork encounters the single-strand nick site in DNA template and collapses to produce a DSB (Kuzminov, 2001; Wimberly et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kuzminov, 2001 and Wimberly et al., 2013 describing this mechanism.

claim: The concurrent introduction of SSB by base editors at the editing site of the HBG1 and HBG2 promoter might generate some 4.9 kb larger deletions, though very few were observed.
source: Based on these findings, we predict the concurrent introduction of SSB by base editors at the editing site of the HBG1 and HBG2 promoter might generate some 4.9 kb larger deletions, though we observed very few.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on inference from the literature and the observed data.

claim: Several different HPFH point mutations have been reported in the HBG promoters; and the effect of these mutations on gamma-globin expression in the native cellular environment has been deciphered for this limited set of mutations.
source: Several different HPFH point mutations have been reported in the HBG promoters; and the effect of these mutations on gamma-globin expression in the native cellular environment has been deciphered for this limited set of mutations (Bauer and Orkin, 2012; Liu et al., 2018; Martyn et al., 2019; Wienert et al., 2017; Wienert et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Bauer and Orkin, 2012; Liu et al., 2018; Martyn et al., 2019; Wienert et al., 2017; Wienert et al., 2015) documenting known HPFH mutations.

claim: Among the known HPFH point mutations, base conversion within the –115 cluster (from –110 to –116) showed the highest increase in promoter activity, confirming previous studies.
source: Among the known HPFH point mutations, base conversion within the –115 cluster (from –110 to –116) showed the highest increase in promoter activity, confirming previous studies (Fucharoen et al., 1990; Gilman et al., 1988; Zertal-Zidani et al., 1999; Motum et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the manuscript and citations to Fucharoen et al., 1990; Gilman et al., 1988; Zertal-Zidani et al., 1999; Motum et al., 1994.

claim: CBE-mediated base conversion (C- to- T) at positions –114 and –115 resulted in a significantly greater induction of HbF than the multiple A-to-G nucleotide substitutions at −110, –112, −113, and –116 positions made by ABE.
source: CBE-mediated base conversion (C- to- T) at positions –114 and –115 resulted in a significantly greater induction of HbF than the multiple A-to-G nucleotide substitutions at −110, –112, −113, and –116 positions made by ABE.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing HbF induction between CBE and ABE at the –115 cluster.

claim: The major HbF repressor BCL11A directly binds to the core TGACC motif located at – 114 to –118.
source: Recently, it has been shown that the major HbF repressor BCL11A directly binds to the core TGACC motif located at – 114 to –118 (Liu et al., 2018; Martyn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2018 and Martyn et al., 2018 documenting BCL11A binding.

claim: Naturally occurring HPFH mutations at –117G > A, –114C > A, –114C > T, –114C > G, and Δ13bp disrupts binding of BCL11A to the promoter.
source: Naturally occurring HPFH mutations at –117G > A, –114C > A, –114C > T, –114C > G, and Δ13bp disrupts binding of BCL11A to the promoter (Martyn et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martyn et al., 2018 documenting these mutations and their effects.

claim: The –113A > G HPFH mutation within the –115 cluster creates a binding site for the master erythroid regulator GATA1 without disrupting the binding of BCL11A.
source: The –113A > G HPFH mutation within the –115 cluster creates a binding site for the master erythroid regulator GATA1 without disrupting the binding of BCL11A (Martyn et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martyn et al., 2019 documenting this mutation and its mechanism.

claim: ABE-mediated T-to-C substitution at position –198 of the HBG gene promoter has previously been shown to be associated with British HPFH and substantially elevates expression of HbF by creating a de novo binding site for the erythroid gene activator KLF1.
source: ABE-mediated T-to-C substitution at position –198 of the HBG gene promoter has previously been shown to be associated with British HPFH and substantially elevates expression of HbF by creating a de novo binding site for the erythroid gene activator KLF1 (Tate et al., 1986; Wienert et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tate et al., 1986 and Wienert et al., 2017 documenting this mutation and its mechanism.

claim: The –175T > C HPFH mutation has been shown to promote enhancer looping to the HBG promoter through recruitment of the activator TAL1.
source: Another known HPFH mutation (–175T > C) has been shown to promote enhancer looping to the HBG promoter through recruitment of the activator TAL1 (Wienert et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wienert et al., 2015 documenting this mutation and its mechanism.

claim: Novel substitutions at –69 (C -to- T), –70 (C- to- T), –122 (G -to -A), –123 (T -to- C), and –124 (T -to -C) of the HBG promoters were identified as potential new regulatory mutations that can elevate gamma-globin expression.
source: In addition to the known mutations, we have identified novel substitutions at –69 (C -to- T), –70 (C- to- T), –122 (G -to -A), –123 (T -to- C), and –124 (T -to -C) of the HBG promoters as potential new regulatory mutations that can elevate gamma-globin expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by the screening data identifying these novel mutations.

claim: The levels of gamma-globin expression resulting from these novel mutations were very similar to those of well-characterized, naturally occurring HPFH mutations.
source: The levels of gamma-globin expression resulting from these mutations were very similar to those of well-characterized, naturally occurring HPFH mutations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing HbF induction levels.

claim: The observation that a de novo KLF1 site formed by the –198T-to-C mutation can upregulate fetal globin raises the possibility that introduction of a KLF1 binding site anywhere around the HBG promoter could potentially upregulate HBG gene expression.
source: This result, together with the observation that a de novo KLF1 site formed by the –198T-to-C mutation can upregulate fetal globin (Tate et al., 1986; Wienert et al., 2017) raises the possibility that introduction of a KLF1 binding site anywhere around the HBG promoter could potentially upregulate HBG gene expression.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on inference from the data and cited literature (Tate et al., 1986; Wienert et al., 2017).

claim: The relative proximity of the –123/–124 site to the BCL11A site, that begins around –117, suggests it may also directly or indirectly affect BCL11A binding.
source: The relative proximity of this site to the BCL11A site, that begins around –117, suggests it may also directly or indirectly affect BCL11A binding.
evidence: This claim is speculation based on the proximity of the sites.

claim: The availability of NGG PAM sequences in the target region confines the resolution of the screening approach.
source: The availability of NGG PAM sequences in the target region confines the resolution of the screening approach.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge about the limitations of PAM-dependent CRISPR systems.

claim: The editing efficiency for ABE7.10 RA or BE3RA-FNLS is not uniform across the target regions.
source: The editing efficiency for ABE7.10 RA or BE3RA-FNLS is not uniform across the target regions (Koblan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Koblan et al., 2018 and data from the manuscript.

claim: The current base editors are mainly involved in the installation of transition mutations, making the effect of transverse mutation in the target region on gene regulation not possible.
source: The effect of transverse mutation in the target region on gene regulation is not possible as the current base editors are mainly involved in the installation of transition mutations (Gaudelli et al., 2017; Komor et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gaudelli et al., 2017 and Komor et al., 2016 describing base editor capabilities.

claim: The bystander mutation introduced by the base editors at the target regions makes it difficult to identify functional regulatory single nucleotides responsible for the gamma-globin regulation.
source: The bystander mutation introduced by the base editors at the target regions makes it difficult to identify functional regulatory single nucleotides responsible for the gamma-globin regulation.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge about base editor limitations and inference from the data.

claim: The translational potential of genome edited HSPCs depends on long-term engraftment and repopulation ability.
source: The translational potential of genome edited HSPCs depends on long-term engraftment and repopulation ability.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about HSPC transplantation requirements.

claim: Genotoxicity and cytotoxicity that can arise as a result of DSBs generated by programmable nucleases can be a limiting factor.
source: However, genotoxicity and cytotoxicity that can arise as a result of DSBs generated by programmable nucleases can be a limiting factor (Cullot et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cullot et al., 2019 and Yu et al., 2016 documenting these concerns.

claim: A previous study in nonhuman primates observed that the HBG promoter editing by Cas9 resulted in HBG2 deletion with up to 27% frequency and that cells with this deletion were under-represented after engraftment.
source: A previous study in nonhuman primates observed that the HBG promoter editing by Cas9 resulted in HBG2 deletion with up to 27% frequency and that cells with this deletion were under-represented after engraftment (Humbert et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Humbert et al., 2019 documenting these findings in nonhuman primates.

claim: Base editing at the target sites of HBG1 and HBG2 promoter by ABE and CBE does not result in high frequency of large deletions in the intergenic region as seen with Cas9 and only showed low levels of indel formation.
source: Base editing at the target sites of HBG1 and HBG2 promoter by ABE and CBE does not result in high frequency of large deletions in the intergenic region as seen with Cas9 and only showed low levels of indel formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing deletion frequencies between base editors and Cas9.

claim: ABEs have an inherent advantage over CBEs as they generate desired edits (A:T to G:C) with high fidelity, whereas the latter generate unanticipated edits.
source: ABEs have an inherent advantage over CBEs as they generate desired edits (A:T to G:C) with high fidelity, whereas the latter generate unanticipated edits.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing product purity between ABE and CBE.

claim: ABE is a better base editor than CBE with respect to purity of base conversion and indel formation, in corroboration with existing findings.
source: In corroboration with existing findings, our results also suggest that ABE is a better base editor than CBE with respect to purity of base conversion and indel formation (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Lee et al., 2018.

claim: The study did not observe any significant DNA and RNA off-target in the ABE and CBE edited cells.
source: Further, our study did not observe any significant DNA and RNA off-target in the ABE and CBE edited cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by off-target analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CRISPR base editing can be utilized to drive the expression of HbF to therapeutically relevant levels in an erythroid progenitor cell line and in HSPCs.
source: In summary, we have demonstrated that CRISPR base editing can be utilized to drive the expression of HbF to therapeutically relevant levels in an erythroid progenitor cell line and in HSPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from HUDEP-2 cells and CD34+ HSPCs.

claim: After screening every gRNAs within the 320 bp region of the HBG promoter, nine gRNAs were identified that, when paired with the appropriate base editor, can introduce HPFH-like mutations without the generation of indels.
source: After screening every gRNAs within the 320 bp region of the HBG promoter, we identified nine gRNAs that, when paired with the appropriate base editor, can introduce HPFH-like mutations without the generation of indels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the screening data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Five novel regulatory regions for HBG1 and HBG2 that are required for the silencing of gamma-globin in adult erythroid cells were identified, shedding light on the molecular mechanisms behind hemoglobin switching.
source: We identified five novel regulatory regions for HBG1 and HBG2 that are required for the silencing of gamma-globin in adult erythroid cells shedding light on the molecular mechanisms behind hemoglobin switching (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by the screening data and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Base editing strategy will be among the pre-eminent therapeutic strategies for monogenetic disorders like beta-hemoglobinopathies in the future.
source: Our work is an exemplification of base editors in mapping gene regulatory elements in highly homologous locus and we hope base editing strategy will be among the pre-eminent therapeutic strategies for monogenetic disorders like beta-hemoglobinopathies in the future.
evidence: This claim is speculation about the future therapeutic potential of base editing.
